observation_summary: The Closure Compiler fails to report a type-checking error when a property is accessed on a record type that does not define it, provided that another unrelated record type in the same scope happens to define that property.
hypothesis: The type-checking algorithm for record types is incorrectly aggregating or leaking property definitions across unrelated record types, causing the compiler to incorrectly conclude that a property exists on a record when it does not.
prediction: The fix will involve modifying the type-checking logic (likely in the property resolution or type inference phase) to ensure that property existence checks are strictly scoped to the specific record type being analyzed, rather than checking a global or shared pool of record properties.
experiment_rationale: The test failure 'expected a warning' confirms that the compiler's type-checking logic is failing to detect an invalid property access. Since this is a logic error in how types are validated against their definitions, it falls under Algorithm/Method.
reasoning_summary: The issue is a failure in the type-checking algorithm to correctly validate property access against the specific record type definition. It is not a missing guard (Checking), nor a simple value assignment error (Assignment/Initialization), nor a design-level capability gap (Function/Class/Object). It is a procedural error in the type-checking logic where properties from unrelated types are incorrectly influencing the validation of the current type.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While the compiler fails to 'check' correctly, the root cause is not a missing guard or boundary condition, but an incorrect implementation of the type-checking algorithm that incorrectly resolves property existence.
The capability to check types exists; the logic within that capability is simply flawed in its implementation of property resolution.
